## Question 1  
 Do you hate Mondays? Researchers in Germany have provided another reason for you: They
concluded that the risk of heart attack on a Monday for a working person may be as much as
50% greater than on any other day.1 The researchers kept track of heart attacks and coronary
arrests over a period of 5 years among 330,000 people who lived near Augsberg, Germany. In an
attempt to verify the researcher’s claim, 200 working people who had recently had heart attacks
were surveyed. The day on which their heart attacks occurred appear in the following table.

\centering
\begin{tabular}{ccccccc}
\hline
Sunday & Monday & Tuesday & Wednesday & Thursday & Friday & Saturday \\
24 & 36 & 27 & 26 & 32 & 26 & 29 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
Do these data present sufficient evidence to indicate that there is a difference in the percentages
of heart attacks that occur on different days of the week? Test using $\alpha = 0.05$.

- Obtain the p-value.

:::


`r bfcolor("ANSWERS TO QUESTION 1:", "red")` \

$$H_0: p_{Sun}=p_{Mon}=p_{Tue}=p_{Wed}=p_{Thu}=p_{Fri}=p_{Sat}= 1/7$$
$$H_a: \text{at least one } p_i \ne 1/7$$
```{r}
n <- 200
p <- 1/7

exp <- n*p
obs <- c(24, 36, 27, 26, 32, 26, 29)

diff <- obs - exp
diff

chisq <- sum(diff^2)/exp
chisq

df <- length(obs) - 1

# Critical Value
crit_val <- qchisq(0.05, df, lower.tail = FALSE)
crit_val

crit_val > chisq # ==> Don't reject H0 if TRUE, Reject H0 if FALSE

# Finding p-value
p_val <- pchisq(chisq, df, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_val
```

**At a significance level $\alpha$ = 0.05, we do not have enough evidence to conclude that there is a difference in the percentages of heart attacks that occur on different days of the week.**

## Question 2  
The data in the following table are the frequency counts for 400 observations on the number
of bacterial colonies within the field of a microscope, using samples of milk film.2 Is there
sufficient evidence to claim that the data do not fit the Poisson distribution? (Use $\alpha = 0.05$.)
	
\textbf{Note:} For the `R` solution, you may use any appropriate built-in function where applicable, **and also** provide your own code to perform the calculations.

\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\hline
\textbf{Number of Colonies per Field} & \textbf{Frequency of Observation} \\
\hline
0  & 56 \\
1  & 104 \\
2  & 80 \\
3  & 62 \\
4  & 42 \\
5  & 27 \\
6  & 9 \\
7  & 9 \\
8  & 5 \\
9  & 3 \\
10 & 2 \\
11 & 0 \\
19 & 1 \\
\hline
   & 400 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

:::

`r bfcolor("ANSWERS TO QUESTION 2:", "red")` \

$$H_0: \text{Data follows a Poisson Distribution}$$
$$H_a: \text{Data DOES NOT follow a Poisson Distribtution}$$
```{r}
# Inputting Data
counts <- c(rep(0, 56), rep(1, 104), rep(2, 80), rep(3, 62), 
            rep(4, 42), rep(5, 27), rep(6, 9), rep(7, 9), rep(8, 5), 
            rep(9, 3), rep(10, 2), rep(19, 1))

n <- length(counts)

freq <- table(counts)

obs_freq <- c(freq["0"], freq["1"], freq["2"], freq["3"], freq["4"],
              freq["5"], freq["6"], sum(freq[as.numeric(names(freq)) >= 7]))

result <- data.frame(
  Yi = c("0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7+"),
  Frequency = as.numeric(obs_freq))

result

# Lambda MLE
lambda_MLE <- sum(counts) / n

# Estimating Frequencies Under H0 (using Lambda MLE) (Must be larger than 5)
exp0 <- dpois(0, lambda_MLE) * n
exp1 <- dpois(1, lambda_MLE) * n
exp2 <- dpois(2, lambda_MLE) * n
exp3 <- dpois(3, lambda_MLE) * n
exp4 <- dpois(4, lambda_MLE) * n
exp5 <- dpois(5, lambda_MLE) * n
exp6 <- dpois(6, lambda_MLE) * n
exp7plus <- n - (exp0 + exp1 + exp2 + exp3 + exp4 + exp5 + exp6)

exp_freq <- c(exp0, exp1, exp2, exp3, exp4, exp5, exp6, exp7plus)
exp_freq

# Pearson ChiSq Test

chisq2 <- sum((obs_freq - exp_freq)^2 / exp_freq)
chisq2

df2 <- length(obs_freq) - 1 - 1 # lost additional df for estimating paramater lambda)

p_val2 <- pchisq(chisq2, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_val2

# Critical Value

crit_val2 <- qchisq(0.05, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)
crit_val2 > chisq2 # TRUE ==> Fail to Reject H0, FALSE ==> Reject H0
crit_val2
```
**Since our p-value is basically 0, at the significance level $\alpha$ = 0.05, we will reject the null hypothesis, that is, we have sufficient evidence to claim that our data DOES NOT follow a Poisson Distribution.**

## Question 3 
 Does education really make a difference in how much money you will earn? Researchers randomly
selected 100 people from each of three income categories—“marginally rich,” “comfortably
rich,” and “super rich”—and recorded their education levels. The data is summarized
in the table that follows.


\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\hline
\textbf{Highest Education Level} & \textbf{Marginally Rich} & \textbf{Comfortably Rich} & \textbf{Super Rich} \\
\hline
No college            & 32 & 20 & 23 \\
Some college          & 13 & 16 & 1  \\
Undergraduate degree  & 43 & 51 & 60 \\
Postgraduate study    & 12 & 13 & 16 \\
\hline
Total & 100 & 100 & 100 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}


\begin{enumerate}
	\item Describe the independent multinomial populations whose proportions are compared in the
$\chi^2$ analysis.

\item Do the data indicate that the proportions in the various education levels differ for the three
income categories? Test at the $\alpha = 0.01$ level.

\end{enumerate}

:::
`r bfcolor("ANSWERS TO QUESTION 3:", "red")` \

**P1:**

Independent Populations - The 3 distinct groups researchers chose to sample, in this case, the Income Categories: Marginally Rich, Comfortably Rich, Super Rich

Multinomial Populations: The 4 mutually exclusive education levels people fall into within the 3 independent populations, the analysis will test whether there is a difference in the education level proportions across the 3 populations: No College, Some College, Undergraduate Degree, Postgraduate Study

**P2:**

$$H_0: \text{The proportion of the 4 education levels is the same across the 3 income categories (Homogenous)}$$
$$H_a: \text{The proportion in the 3 education levels differ across the 3 income categories (Not Homogenous)}$$

```{r}
data <- matrix(c(32, 20, 23,
                 13, 16, 1,
                 43, 51, 60,
                 12, 13, 16),
               nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

colnames(data) <- c("Marginally_Rich", "Comfortably_Rich", "Super_Rich")
rownames(data) <- c("No_College", "Some_College", "Undergraduate", "Postgraduate")

data

# Row Totals
total_row1 <- sum(data[1,])
total_row2 <- sum(data[2,])
total_row3 <- sum(data[3,])
total_row4 <- sum(data[4,])

col_total <- 100 # since sampled 100 people from each income level

grand_total <- 300

# Expected Values

exp_row1 <- (total_row1 * col_total) / grand_total
exp_row2 <- (total_row2 * col_total) / grand_total
exp_row3 <- (total_row3 * col_total) / grand_total
exp_row4 <- (total_row4 * col_total) / grand_total

# Test Statistic
chisq3 <- sum((data[1,] - exp_row1)^2 / exp_row1) + sum((data[2,] - exp_row2)^2 / exp_row2) +
  sum((data[3,] - exp_row3)^2 / exp_row3) + sum((data[4,] - exp_row4)^2 / exp_row4)
chisq3

df3 <- (nrow(data) - 1)*(ncol(data) - 1)

# P-value and Critical Value

p_val3 <- pchisq(chisq3, df3, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_val3
  
crit_val3 <- qchisq(0.01, df3, lower.tail = FALSE)
crit_val3 > chisq3 # TRUE ==> Fail to Reject H0, FALSE ==> Reject H0
crit_val3
```
**At the significance level $\alpha$ = 0.01, our critical value is 16.81189 which is smaller than our observed test statistic of 19.172, which means we are within the rejection region and thus, will reject H0. That is, we have sufficient evidence to say that there is a difference in the education level proportions across the 3 income categories.**

## Question 4 

The results of a study suggest that the initial electrocardiogram (ECG) of a suspected heart
attack victim can be used to predict in-hospital complications of an acute nature. The study
included 469 patients with suspected myocardial infarction (heart attack). Each patient was
categorized according to whether their initial ECG was positive or negative and whether the
person suffered life-threatening complications subsequently in the hospital. The results are
summarized in the following table.


\centering
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\hline
 & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{Subsequent In-Hospital Life-Threatening Complications}} & \\
\cline{2-3}
\textbf{ECG} & \textbf{No} & \textbf{Yes} & \textbf{Total} \\
\hline
Negative & 166 & 1  & 167 \\
Positive & 260 & 42 & 302 \\
\hline
Total & 426 & 43 & 469 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}


Is there sufficient evidence to indicate that whether or not a heart attack patient suffers
complications depends on the outcome of the initial ECG? Test using $\alpha = 0.05$.
:::

`r bfcolor("ANSWERS TO QUESTION 4:", "red")` \

```{r}
               nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

rownames(data2) <- c("Negative", "Positive")

chisq.test(data2)
```
